notes.meaning: The people encourage one another to turn back to the Lord in the middle of their suffering. They recognize that God allowed them to be broken and hurt because of their sins. Even so, they trust that He wounds only to heal and restore anyone who comes back to Him.

God promises to bring His people out of their misery quickly, as if raising them from the dead. Even when their situation looks completely hopeless, His help will not be delayed for long. Christians also see here a picture of Jesus Christ being raised from the dead on the third day.

differ.view: Lutherans traditionally see this verse as a direct prophecy foretelling the bodily resurrection of Jesus on the third day.
Many Reformed teachers see the verse primarily as God promising quick national rescue to Israel, with Christ's resurrection serving as the great illustration of how God gives life to His people.

notes.meaning: The people urge one another to press forward in learning to know and obey the Lord. They are confident that God will show up to help them just as surely as the dawn breaks every morning. His arrival will refresh their parched lives like gentle spring rains soaking dry ground.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: The Latter Rain Movement used this verse to teach that God would bring a special end-times spiritual outpouring, restoring modern apostles and prophets to the church.

notes.meaning: God speaks with deep sorrow to both Ephraim and Judah about their shallow repentance. Any goodness or loyalty they showed quickly melted away, just like early morning mist or morning dew that vanishes under the sun. Their hearts were so unsteady that they kept turning right back to their sins.

Because the people were stubborn, God sent His prophets to deliver cutting and painful warnings. The strong messages of judgment from God's mouth struck them down to expose their guilt. God's decisions were entirely fair and plain for everyone to see, shining out like bright daylight.

God explains what He truly wants from His people: active love, mercy, and a genuine relationship with Him. The people were offering animal sacrifices at the altar, but they treated others poorly and ignored God in daily life. Rituals and religious ceremonies are useless to God when the heart has no love or obedience.

Israel broke the holy covenant, which was God's sacred agreement with them, just as Adam did in the beginning. Even though God gave them a good land and wonderful promises, they turned away and proved unfaithful. Right there in the home God provided for them, they chose to act like traitors.

differ.view: Many in the Reformed tradition point to this verse as clear biblical proof that God made a covenant of works with Adam in the Garden of Eden, which Adam broke.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars note that the phrase can be translated as breaking a covenant like ordinary men do, or even as breaking faith at a specific town called Adam in the Jordan Valley.

notes.meaning: The city of Gilead had become famous for violence and wicked behavior. Even though parts of it were set apart as a safe refuge and a home for priests, it was covered in bloody footprints. Those who were supposed to teach God's law were actively guilty of murder and injustice.

A group of priests banded together like highway robbers to ambush and kill travelers on the road to Shechem. Rather than helping people on their way to worship, the religious leaders plotted evil schemes together. Their crimes were done on purpose and showed how deeply corrupt the priesthood had become.

God looked over the northern kingdom of Israel and saw terrible, repulsive wickedness. The people were running after idols, which God viewed as spiritual unfaithfulness or prostitution against Him. This widespread false worship made the entire land unclean in God's eyes.

The southern kingdom of Judah was warned that an appointed time of harvest was coming for them as well. Because they sowed the same sins as Israel, they would eventually reap God's judgment and go into captivity. Even so, God looked ahead to a future day when He would turn things around and restore His people.
